item.text: The Crime and Corruption Commission compared corruption perceptions across Queensland community members, public sector employees, council employees and police service employees to inform prevention and planning.
item.support:
so the CCC can 
monitor the impact of its prevention agenda and 
inform future strategic planning.

item.text: The analysis used 10,059 completed surveys collected in March to May 2025, with weighting applied to the community sample but not the employee samples.
item.support:
In total, 16,218 surveys were commenced across four cohorts, 
with 10,059 surveys completed.

item.text: The CCC found that all groups felt more comfortable reporting to it than to the relevant workplace or government agency, while retaliation and inaction were shared concerns.
item.support:
For all cohorts, the top two 
concerns surrounding reporting corruption relate to an 
expectation there may be backlash or retaliation

item.text: The CCC reported that council employees were comparatively more comfortable with workplace reporting, while police service employees expressed lower trust in the CCC and lower expectations of meaningful action.
item.support:
Local council employees tend to hold a more 
positive view of how corruption is managed, 
particularly within their workplace.

item.quote:
There is, however, also a shared concern as 
to whether or not meaningful action would be taken if 
corruption were to be reported.

There is, however, consistently lower 
agreement across employee cohorts that their workplace 
culture supports reporting corruption.
